paragraphs.text: This is Tieguanyin made into a [scented tea](tieguanyin:osmanthus). Osmanthus flowers, picked in autumn, are layered with the finished leaf in rounds so the leaf takes up their scent, and the tea is then dried again. Two harvests meet in one tea: the leaf's own and the flowers'.

[Tieguanyin](tieguanyin:definition) is both a tea plant and the [oolong](oolong:definition) made from it. Its home is Anxi County in southern Fujian, where the name is protected, and the name itself joins iron with Guanyin, the bodhisattva of mercy. To make it, the leaf is shaken and rested until its edges turn red around a green middle, the [green leaf with a red rim](tieguanyin:making). It is then fixed, wrapped in cloth and rolled again and again, each round tightening it, until it closes into the small balls you see here.

brewing.text: Tieguanyin is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C; the light green style is often taken a little cooler, about 85 to 95°C. Use about 4 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 150 ml gaiwan or pot, about a third full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 10 to 30 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and a good Tieguanyin gives about six to eight. In a larger pot, use about 2.5 to 5 grams for 240 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: In the light style: orchid and other flowers, a fresh, clean cup and a sweet aftertaste. In the roasted style: toast and charcoal, caramel or honey, stone or dried fruit, nuts, and a liquor that runs from gold to amber.
